extracted.intended_audience: readers of art history; painters, sculptors, architects and their patrons (Renaissance/early-modern Italian context)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and aesthetic/technical standards used to judge the quality of painting, sculpture, and architecture in Vasari's Lives (Renaissance Italian practices), including matters of draughtsmanship, imitation of the ancients, invention, materials, and structural technique. The guidance mixes aesthetic judgement with practical/technical notes and historical examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation of the ancient
rubrics_metrics.description: Turned to imitating the ancient with all their industry and wit; the 'ancient' are the works made before Constantine (Corinth, Athens, Rome etc.), as opposed to the 'old' (post‑Silvester remnant Greeks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vasari treats imitation of ancient models as a major corrective to the rude modern manner—he traces an improvement c.1250 when artists abandoned the crude contemporary style and 'turned to imitating the ancient.' Examples: renewed attention to classical forms in architecture and sculpture, drawing on remains of Roman arches, colossi, statues, urns, and storied columns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draughtsmanship (drawing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Excellence in draughtsmanship is repeatedly praised as foundational to good painting: 'how much excellence was given by his work to draughtsmanship.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vasari stresses precise line and drawing as essential; he notes that drawings and portraits often show more about a craftsman than prose can. He also warns that engravers (without draughtsmanship) 'rob the faces' of minute features. Examples: Cimabue's miniatures and collected drawings showing his draughtsmanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty and freshness of colouring
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty of colouring and the freshness of colours (particularly in flesh tones) indicate technical advancement in painting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vasari cites the 'freshness of the colours in the flesh' in Cimabue's frescoes at Assisi as evidence that painting made great progress. Colour is evaluated both for its vibrancy and for its contribution to naturalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Painting from nature / naturalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Portraying figures 'from nature' rather than merely following conventional outlines is a sign of superior art: 'portrayed him from nature (which was something new in those times).'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vasari commends observation of real models (e.g., Cimabue's life-portrayal of St Francis) and praises works where attitudes, gestures, and physiognomy are rendered more lifelike. This is presented as a break from the schematic 'eyes staring, hands outstretched' medieval manner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention and novelty of composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventive composition, new methods of expression, and original conception are valued: 'he began to give light and to open the way to invention.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vasari highlights novel devices (e.g., using words in the painting to express conception) and fresh narrative arrangements. Invention is scored positively when it advances clarity, expression, or naturalism rather than being merely whimsical ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design of figures and draperies (attitude & method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Graceful, lively, and natural attitudes and the treatment of draperies show improved method and invention ('beautiful method in the attitude of a Madonna... folds of the draperies... more lively and more natural and softer').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how convincingly the figure's pose and the fall of drapery articulate form and movement. Good examples: Cimabue's panels where Madonna and Child attitudes and draperies depart from the rigid Greek manner toward softer, more lifelike rendering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fresco execution and placement (durability & preservation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality of fresco technique and the survival of works in situ are indicators of excellence: roof/ceiling paintings are often better preserved and show the artist's hand more clearly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vasari notes that vaulting work (being less injured by dust and accidents) preserves the 'freshness of the colours' better than lower walls. Judge fresco by technique, pigments (e.g., ultramarine), and compositional clarity on architectural surfaces (vaults, medallions, sections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of classical materials/spoils and mouldings
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporating ancient spoils and classical mouldings can display recovery of good design: 'from the walls ... made from ancient spoils ... it is seen that the art was going on continually improving.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vasari considers the intelligent reuse or emulation of classical elements (mouldings, columns) as evidence of striving toward the good; such features should be in dialogue with classical proportion and design rather than chaotic eclecticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion and reasonable order
rubrics_metrics.description: Just and reasonable proportion and order are essential; deviation into extravagant, barbaric, or disproportionate inventions is criticized ('almost wide of all just and reasonable proportion').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether mouldings, capitals, column shafts, and sculptural groups observe harmonious proportion. Vasari criticizes Marchionne's 'whimsical variety' when it departs from classical proportion. Good work shows considered proportion, not mere novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundations, engineering, and structural soundness
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper foundations and engineering practice (e.g., use of piles in Pisa) are required for durable architecture; poor founding leads to inclination or failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vasari uses the leaning Campanile of Pisa as a technical case: lack of piles/support caused sinking; additions (outworks) later used to support it. Evaluate architects on sound founding methods, knowledge of soil, appropriate structural solutions (foundations, binding stones), and whether the building's form aids stability (e.g., round vs. square plan).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of sculptural relief and ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Sculptural work must show good design, proportion, and tasteful relief; crude or 'barbaric' low/half-relief ornament is decried as misshapen and gross.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vasari cites many examples of rude low-reliefs and barbaric arch carvings as anti-patterns. Good sculptural ornament supports architectural logic, uses appropriate relief depth, and displays lifelike modelling and classical reference rather than grotesque distortion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding mere extravagance over true excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: Buildings praised for extravagance rather than design are suspect: 'this campanile is praised, not because it has in it any design or beautiful manner, but simply for its extravagance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether impressive effects (scale, novelty) serve real architectural/aesthetic merit or are empty spectacle. Preference is given to lasting artistic and technical merit rather than foolhardy or novelty-driven ostentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and medium-appropriate portraiture
rubrics_metrics.description: Portrait likeness depends on age, medium, and technical skill: 'the portrait made of a man when he was eighteen or twenty years old will never be like to the portrait ... fifteen or twenty years later' and 'portraits in drawing are never so like as are those in colours.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge portraiture by sitter likeness over time, and by medium—colour painting typically produces truer likeness than drawing or engravings by non-draughtsmen. Beware of limitations introduced by reproduction techniques (engravings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Apprenticeship, teaching, and transmission of craft
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper apprenticeship and the transmission of skill from masters to pupils is essential for progress: Cimabue apprenticed to Greek masters, then trained Giotto; the master's labours 'kept [the art] alive' and produced improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vasari values the social/institutional aspect of craft: judge workshops by their ability to transmit draughtsmanship, invention, and technique. A strong pedagogical lineage (master → successful disciple) is an indicator of a healthy artistic method.
